**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Philosophy 2 (0790), Paper 2 (Philosophical Culture), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2020. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are expected to answer FOUR (04) questions chosen from the three sections imperatively (at least ONE question from each section). Each question carries 25 marks.

Each essay must contain: an introduction = 5 marks; a thesis = 7 marks; an antithesis = 6 marks; a synthesis = 3 marks; a conclusion = 4 marks.

Candidates are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation of material.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Critically examine the Sartrean view that: "Existence precedes essence."

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** "Existence precedes essence" is the central thesis of Jean-Paul Sartre's existentialism, set out in his lecture *Existentialism is a Humanism* and developed in *Being and Nothingness*. To examine it critically means to state what it says, to show on what it rests, and to weigh its strengths and its weaknesses. The problem is whether a human being has no nature given in advance and is entirely what he makes of himself.

**Thesis: the Sartrean view and its justification.**
(i) *Meaning.* The essence of a thing is what it is (its definition, nature, purpose); its existence is the plain fact that it is there. For manufactured objects essence comes first: Sartre's example is the paper-knife, which the craftsman conceives (its purpose and method of making) before he makes it. Traditional philosophy and religion thought of man in the same way, as made according to a concept in the mind of God (the view of the Scholastics, and in a different form of Descartes and Leibniz), so that a human nature is given to all. Sartre, who defends an atheistic existentialism, says that if there is no God there is no one to conceive man in advance. Man first exists, turns up in the world, encounters himself, and only afterwards defines himself by what he does. At the beginning he is nothing; he becomes what he makes of himself.
(ii) *Consequences.* (a) Man is radically free: he is "condemned to be free", because he did not create himself and yet is free, and cannot escape choosing, since refusing to choose is also a choice. (b) Man is responsible: he cannot blame God, nature, heredity or society; in choosing for himself he chooses an image of man for everyone, which produces anguish. (c) Bad faith: pretending to be a fixed thing (the waiter who is only a waiter, the person who says "that is my nature") is self-deception that denies one's freedom. Authenticity is to accept freedom and responsibility. (d) Human dignity: man is a project, not an object.
(iii) *Merits.* The view defends freedom and responsibility against excuses based on fate or temperament; it fits the experience of deciding and of making oneself; and it rejects fixed stereotypes of race, class or sex that have been used to justify oppression (Simone de Beauvoir used the same idea in saying that one is not born a woman but becomes one).

**Antithesis: objections to the Sartrean view.**
(i) *Facticity and conditioning.* Man is born with a body, genes, a language, a family, a social class and a history that he did not choose. Marx held that social conditions shape consciousness; Freud that the unconscious drives much of our behaviour; modern biology and psychology show real limits. Sartre admits facticity but treats it as the raw material of choice; critics reply that he still overstates our freedom.
(ii) *An implicit essence.* Sartre denies a human nature but speaks of a "human condition" (to be born, to work, to die, to live among others) and ascribes to every man freedom and anguish. Critics say that this is a human essence under another name.
(iii) *The atheistic premise.* The thesis depends on the absence of God, which Sartre assumes more than proves. Theistic thinkers (Thomists, Gabriel Marcel, and Christian existentialists such as Kierkegaard, who also stressed existence) reject it and keep a purpose given by the Creator.
(iv) *Community.* African thought, for example Mbiti and Menkiti, holds that a person becomes a person through the community, language, rites and relations with others. Self-creation by a solitary choosing individual neglects this. Sartre does treat the other, but mainly as a source of conflict (the look).
(v) *Moral guidance.* If there is no given human nature and no given value, a choice seems arbitrary. Sartre replies that the individual must choose as if for all mankind and in an authentic way, but his own example of the pupil torn between caring for his mother and joining the Resistance shows that no rule can settle the matter in advance.

**Synthesis.** The thesis is sound as a defence of freedom, responsibility and the refusal of fixed labels; it is exaggerated if it denies every given element. A more balanced view holds that existence and essence are both involved: we start with given limits (body, culture, community) and we shape our identity by our choices within them.

**Conclusion.** Sartre's claim that "existence precedes essence" has lasting value because it makes man the author of his own life, but it cannot be accepted without qualification, since man's freedom is conditioned by nature, by society and by the community that forms him.
